nameStory: American pennyroyal gets its name from its old medicinal use as a penny's worth of 'royal' herb - a common folk remedy that was affordable to even the poorest people. The 'American' part distinguishes it from European pennyroyal, a different but related mint that was brought to the New World by colonists.
description: American pennyroyal is a small, scrappy annual plant that rarely grows taller than a foot. This native mint has a branching, square stem and tiny narrow leaves that pack a powerful aromatic punch when crushed. In late summer, it produces clusters of pale blue flowers that are small but numerous, giving the plant a delicate, airy appearance despite its strong personality.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Crush a leaf between your fingers - the intense, sharp minty smell is unmistakable and much stronger than most other wild mints. The leaves are small, thin, and narrow with a pungent taste.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that reaches only 6-12 inches tall with multiple branches spreading out from the base, creating a somewhat bushy but delicate appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale blue flowers appear in small clusters along the stem in mid to late summer. Each flower is less than a quarter-inch long but they're numerous enough to be noticeable.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that are typical of the mint family, often with fine hairs and multiple branches. The stem feels firm but not woody when rolled between your fingers.

habitat: Look for American pennyroyal in dry, sandy soils and open areas like fields, roadsides, and woodland edges. It prefers disturbed ground and doesn't compete well in dense vegetation, so you'll often find it in clearings or areas with sparse grass coverage.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants begin growing as small rosettes with the characteristic square stems just beginning to show.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their pale blue flowers from mid-summer through late summer, filling the air with their distinctive minty fragrance.
seasonality.fall: After flowering, plants set seed and begin to die back. The strong scent remains in dried plant material even after the first frosts kill the plant.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: This little plant was so abundant in western Kentucky that it gave its name to an entire geographic region - the Pennyroyal Plateau - where early settlers found it growing in such profusion that the whole landscape smelled minty on warm days!
confusionNotes: Other small wild mints might look similar, but none have American pennyroyal's incredibly intense, almost harsh minty smell. If you crush a leaf and don't get hit with a powerful aromatic blast that makes your eyes water a bit, it's probably not pennyroyal.
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the name 'pennyroyal' with a European mint, American pennyroyal is in a completely different genus and is much milder in its effects. The many folk names like 'mosquito plant' and 'tickweed' hint at its traditional use as an insect repellent.
compareHints: American pennyroyal is the only member of the Hedeoma genus commonly found in New England, though Rough False Pennyroyal occurs further west. Compared to other small mints in the region, pennyroyal is distinguished by its annual growth habit, extremely potent scent, and preference for dry, disturbed soils rather than the moist areas favored by most mints.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rough false pennyroyal differs from its close relative American pennyroyal primarily in texture and flower arrangement - American pennyroyal has smooth leaves and flowers arranged in more obvious clusters at the stem tips.
